title: Assessment of global dimming and brightening in IPCC-AR4/CMIP3 models and ERA40
problem: Climate models and reanalyses struggle to accurately reproduce observed decadal variations in surface solar radiation ("global dimming" and "brightening"), as they significantly underestimate the magnitude of these changes and often fail to capture the correct qualitative trends.
method: This paper presents a method for evaluating climate models by comparing simulated surface solar radiation against observational records, creating composite anomaly time series for five regions, and using polynomial fits to assess the reproduction of decadal dimming and brightening trends.
task: The task is to evaluate the ability of CMIP3/IPCC-AR4 climate models and the ERA40 reanalysis to reproduce observed decadal variations in surface solar radiation ("global dimming" and "brightening") by using observational records from the Global Energy Balance Archive.

innovation: This paper evaluates 23 IPCC-AR4/CMIP3 climate models and the ERA40 reanalysis, demonstrating that they largely fail to reproduce the qualitative trends and consistently underestimate the magnitude of observed decadal variations in surface solar radiation ("global dimming" and "brightening") across five major world regions.

The linear trends in the models between 1960 and 1985 vary from -0.183 Wm-2a¯¹ in the GFDL-CM2.0 model to 0.173 Wm-2a¯¹ in the IPSL-CM4, with a multi-model mean slope -0.012 Wm¯²a¯¹. None of the models thus captures the observed decrease quantitatively.

The individual model deviations are further quantified in terms of the root mean squared error (RMS) of the simulated compared to the observed SSR composite time series (Table 5). The RMS statistics have been determined based on the 5-year running means of the time series, since climate models cannot expected to be deterministic on short interannual time-scales, and deviations induced by these year-to-year variations are therefore meaningless.

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: correlation of simulated and observed all-sky SSR
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: All correlations are based on the time series smoothed with 5-year running means, to compare the lower frequency variations in models and observations rather than the interannual variations which are not deterministic in GCMs. Interestingly, correlations are typically higher when the (all-sky) observations are correlated with the simulated clear-sky fluxes than with the simulated all-sky fluxes (Table 6). This applies for 14 out of the 19 models that provide both all-sky and clear-sky fluxes.

In contrast to Southeast China, the observed composite time series, based on seven sites in Northwest China, does not show a strong recovery in the 1990s. Therefore the continuous decrease over the entire period can be reasonably approximated with a first order linear polynomial.

Similarly to the region in Northwest China, the observed radiation records in India show a continuous decrease in SSR from 1964 to 2000 with no substantial recovery in the more recent period (Wild et al. 2005; Ramanathan et al. 2005; Kumari et al. 2007; Ohmura 2009).
